claims.text: The target material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy.
The target alloy has a high-entropy FCC matrix.
The starting microstructure contains a stable distribution of strengthening precipitates produced by additive manufacturing.
The as-built material has homogeneous mechanical properties before elevated-temperature exposure.
The proposed controlled intervention is to vary oxygen partial pressure between oxidizing and reducing atmospheres while holding the thermal exposure fixed.
The proposed mechanism applies at approximately 900 °C and above.
Exposure durations longer than about 100 hours allow significant oxide formation in this alloy.
Oxidizing environments promote rapid oxide-scale formation in the target alloy.
Oxides form preferentially along grain boundaries and at matrix–precipitate interfaces.
The oxide scales formed under oxidizing conditions are brittle and have a high volume fraction.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between oxide scales and the alloy induces local strain during thermal cycling.
Oxide-associated local stress concentrations increase creep deformation.
Oxide-associated stresses initiate microcracks along grain boundaries and interfaces.
Reducing environments produce minimal oxide growth relative to oxidizing environments.
Reduced oxide growth slows stress accumulation and delays microstructural degradation.
Coalescence of oxide-induced microcracks causes catastrophic intergranular failure.
Oxidizing exposure will produce thicker and more continuous grain-boundary oxide scales than reducing exposure.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a higher grain-boundary and interface crack density than reducing exposure.
Oxidizing exposure will accelerate losses in tensile and creep properties and cause earlier catastrophic failure relative to reducing exposure.

The mechanism is falsified if oxidizing exposure does not increase oxide thickness or continuity, crack density, or mechanical-property degradation relative to the reducing control, or if failure does not correlate with oxide-induced microcracking.

contradictions.description: The baseline field defines the baseline as the initial as-built state, whereas the predicted outcome refers to the oxidizing condition as the baseline. This makes the intended reference condition inconsistent.
